speaker: Ms Anthea Ong
text: asked the Minister for Home Affairs (a) what are the criteria used to determine whether Singaporean individuals, firms or media organisations are at risk of being compromised by foreign influence for national security reasons; (b) whether a list of such individuals or organisations at risk, and the reasons for these risks, will be published; and (c) whether positions that involve media, communications or outreach that address issues of social or political concern should be staffed exclusively by Singaporeans due to the risks of foreign influence.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira
text: asked the Minister for Home Affairs (a) what are the facts behind the concerns expressed at the recent Foreign Interference Tactics and Countermeasures Conference that certain activists and media persons are potential agents of foreign influence; and (b) how can Singaporeans protect themselves against foreign influence given that association with and receiving income from foreign sources are common amongst globalised Singapore firms and individuals.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Often, this is done for money; sometimes, for other reasons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I am not sure you can do this, identify this by specific criteria.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It really depends on what is actually done, what actually happens.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The cases of Eastern Sun and Singapore Herald are illustrative.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In fact, I am a little perplexed by the question because how do you make a comprehensive list of all people who may potentially be recruited by foreign agencies or be subject to foreign influence?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: When I put it in those terms, you can see that the point is quite absurd.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: In foreign countries, even Members of Parliament have been recruited by foreign agencies.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, it will be quite meaningless to publish such lists.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Whether we should identify specific areas which are more likely to be vectors for foreign influence and have some better way of managing those risks – given that the environment is changing – that is a different issue.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Of course, there are specific jobs that already have requirements for security clearances for these and other reasons.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: If action is, in fact, taken against a particular individual or organisation, the case often becomes public.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: This will be so unless there are national security reasons not to reveal the details.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Nominated Member will be aware, for example, of the case involving Mr Huang Jing.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Nominated Member of Parliament has also asked about controlling the employment of foreigners in organisations involving media, communications, outreach.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I assume she is referring to my statement on 25 September at the Foreign Interference Tactics and Countermeasures Conference.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will say we have to look at the issue from a broader perspective, for example, the nature of the organisation, the confidence that we can have that the employees are likely to be immune to foreign influence, that there are controls, and also our own ability to identify any possible foreign influence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will next address Nominated Member of Parliament Walter Theseira's questions.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He asked about the facts behind the concerns expressed at that Conference.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The facts which led to me as well as others expressing concerns can be found in my speech as well as in the presentations made by some of the other speakers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A transcript of the speech is on my Home Ministry's website and I have asked my officers to send a link of it to the Nominated Member of Parliament.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have also asked my officers to send him the material that was presented at the Conference.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: On the second part of the Member's question, I think the Nominated Member of Parliament may have misunderstood what I have said.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I will also refer as an example to some of the statements made at the congressional hearings held on 7 December 2018, 24 July 2019 and 26 September 2019 in the United States.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I have attached a short list of quotes made at that hearing that the Nominated Member of Parliament may find useful and, with your permission, Mr Speaker, may I ask the Clerk to distribute those handouts?

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I was not aware that the Minister has finished his statement.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I share the Minister's concerns about foreign influence risk.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I think my only supplementary question is that I wish to ask if the Minister would agree that in assessing these kinds of foreign influence risk, we should look more at the facts of what these persons are doing in terms of their actions, their writings, points of views expressed and so forth, at their actions and behaviours and perhaps less at whether they, for example, just received foreign funding or employ foreigners in sensitive positions.

speaker: Assoc Prof Walter Theseira (Nominated Member)
text: I am concerned because if we are too quick to judge on these matters, we may deter Singaporeans from engaging in foreign exchanges, international exchanges and so forth, and that is going to be very important for us as a globalised society.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think what the Nominated Member of Parliament has said is one part of it.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: First, the current law is that in certain categories, there is no foreign influence allowed whatsoever.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: For example, in order to be a Member of Parliament – obvious.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Equally, Members of Parliament, political parties are not allowed to take donations from foreign agencies, other foreigners.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, the Nominated Member of Parliament's point does not quite deal with the issues.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Certain types, certain categories of positions, organisations like political parties which seek to contest and represent the viewpoints of Singaporeans must not accept money from foreign institutions, and it is no answer to say, "Oh, you should not prevent Singaporeans from engaging with international opinions." There is nothing to prevent politicians, political parties from engaging with foreign parties, but you cannot take money from them.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You need to identify what it is that we are speaking about.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then, in certain other areas, for example, newspapers, we do not allow foreigners to control or fund newspapers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: That is in the Newspaper and Printing Presses Act (NPPA).

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But if I were to put it in broader terms, we want to keep foreign influence out of our political environment, not allow foreigners to influence our own political processes and we have crafted a series of laws over the years.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I think Singaporeans accept that and the quotes that I gave you would show to you that the Americans accept that as well.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: I do not think that is really arguable.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: How that should be applied in specific cases, we can always discuss.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: A local businessman, Aw Kow – he is son of one of the Tiger Balm brothers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He approached senior officials of a news agency from communist China – it was based on Hong Kong – for money.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Eastern Sun faced financial problems soon after it began operations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The communist officials injected another HK$1.2 million with an added condition that Aw appoint their representative as adviser to the newspaper and Aw agreed to that.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Government exposed this in May of 1971.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Eastern Sun's senior editorial staff resigned en masse.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The newspaper ceased publication a few days later.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The Eastern Sun was a case of black ops.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It was an attempt by communist China to capture and manipulate the local media, ultimately to influence public opinion and create a political situation favourable to their own interests.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Communists even allowed the newspaper to take an anti-communist line.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: As the former Prime Minister Lee Kuan Yew pointed out, this reflected their long-term approach and patience so that, ultimately, they have an agent, they have an institution of influence.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Certain categories of jobs, certain categories of operations, media, are commonly used as vectors.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: You need to look at it very carefully and you cannot say, "Oh, we need to interact with the people from overseas and, therefore, it is okay." It is not okay to go and take money to run a foreign country's agenda in Singapore.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: English newspaper, started in July 1970, used as a tool for foreign interference in the 1970s.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Its editorials played up issues relating to, for example, National Service, that it should be done away with.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: The supposed shareholders were a former Chief Minister of Sabah, a Hong Kong businesswoman and a foreign bank.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Then Prime Minister Lee and Foreign Minister Rajaratnam met with the Hong Kong businesswoman, Aw Sian, and Singapore Herald's managing director, Jimmy Hahn, as well as the editor, Ambrose Khaw.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr Lee asked them about the finances of the paper.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Aw Sian gave the initial financing of $500,000.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She said she had no knowledge of the financial standing of the paper.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She said that the $500,000 was her money.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, Mr Lee Kuan Yew asked her, if you know nothing about the newspaper and you do not know how it is doing, how come you are sending this money in, if it was your money?

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: She apparently gave the money on the basis of three receipts and had no control over the Singapore Herald.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: There were considerable doubts on the part of our intelligence agencies and the local Chase Manhattan branch gave overdraft facilities to the Singapore Herald and that was contrary to Chase Manhattan's policy.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Mr David Rockefeller, the chairman of Chase Manhattan, told Prime Minister Lee in May 1971 that the bank had a standing rule of not lending money to newspapers.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: He claimed that Hendrik Kwant, the manager in Singapore, did not know of this standing rule and approved the overdraft to the Singapore Herald.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: So, you can see it is equal opportunity.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It is not just one country or another.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: It can be maintained without saying, "Therefore, we cannot interact with people outside of Singapore".

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: Whether it is in business or in the academia or in politics, we must keep track, interact and understand what is going on and have deep relationships.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: But that is different from taking money from people or allowing people to influence operations.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And we in this House should stand against that.

speaker: Ms Anthea Ong (Nominated Member)
text: I am sorry that I perplexed him and that he found my question absurd.

speaker: Mr K Shanmugam
text: And I had not suggested that the Member's question was absurd, but I had said any suggestion would be absurd.
